name: Sumer and Akkad
line: The first cities and the first writing, in the land between the Tigris and Euphrates.
tie: Ibrahim grew up among the city gods of its heirs, and broke their idols (21:51-58).

name: Ancient Egypt
line: Three thousand years of pharaohs, pyramids and temples along the Nile.
tie: The Quran tells of Yusuf over its storehouses and of Musa facing its Firaun, 'owner of the stakes' (89:10).

name: Indus Valley
line: A Bronze Age civilisation of planned brick cities in today's Pakistan and India.
tie: Its land became Sindh, where Islam arrived with Muhammad ibn Qasim in 711.

name: Babylonia
line: The kingdom of Hammurabi and Nebuchadnezzar, centred on the city of Babylon.
tie: The Quran names Babylon as the place where Harut and Marut were sent as a trial (2:102).

name: Shang and Zhou China
line: China's early dynasties and warring states, whose bronze, writing and thinkers shaped East Asia.
tie: The Quran says no nation was left without a warner (35:24), though it names none in China.

name: Assyria
line: A warrior empire of northern Iraq that conquered from Egypt to Iran.
tie: Its capital Nineveh is the city of Yunus, whose people believed and were spared (10:98).

name: Saba (Sheba)
line: A rich kingdom of incense, caravans and great dams in Yemen.
tie: The Quran tells of its queen coming to Sulayman and of the flood from its broken dam (27:22-44, 34:15-17).

name: Kingdom of Dawud and Sulayman
line: The united kingdom of Bani Israil under the prophet-kings Dawud and Sulayman, and the kingdoms that followed.
tie: Allah gave Dawud kingship and prophethood (2:251), and Sulayman a kingdom like no other (38:35).

name: Greek city-states
line: City-states of philosophers, theatre and science around the Aegean.
tie: Muslim scholars in Baghdad translated Aristotle and Euclid and kept Greek learning alive.

name: Persian Empire
line: Cyrus's empire, the largest the world had yet seen.
tie: Cyrus freed the Jews from Babylon; some scholars identify him with Dhul-Qarnayn (18:83), others disagree.

name: Alexander and successors
line: Alexander's conquests and the Greek kingdoms that divided his empire.
tie: Some later writers identified Alexander with Dhul-Qarnayn, but many scholars reject this because he was a pagan.

name: Han China
line: China's great early empire, which opened the Silk Road.
tie: The Silk Road it opened later carried Muslim merchants, and Islam, into China.

name: Roman Empire
line: The empire of the Mediterranean, which ruled Jerusalem in the time of Isa and later became Christian.
tie: Isa was born under Roman rule, and Rome destroyed the Temple in Jerusalem in 70 CE.

name: Himyar (Yemen)
line: The last great kingdom of ancient Yemen, whose kings turned to Judaism.
tie: The Quran's people of Tubba (44:37) and the Companions of the Ditch (85:4) belong to Himyar's story.

name: Sasanian Persia
line: Persia's last Zoroastrian empire, rival of Rome for four centuries.
tie: Its war with Rome opens Surah al-Rum (30:2-4), and it fell to the Muslims by 651.

name: Byzantine Empire
line: The Christian Roman Empire, ruled from Constantinople for a thousand years.
tie: The Quran foretold its victory over Persia (30:2-4); the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453.

name: Aksum (Abyssinia)
line: A Christian trading kingdom in today's Ethiopia and Eritrea.
tie: Its just king, the Najashi, sheltered the first Muslim emigrants in 615.

name: Empire of Ghana
line: A West African empire grown rich on the gold trade across the Sahara.
tie: Muslim merchants had their own town beside its capital, and Islam spread through its lands after the Almoravids.

name: Tang China
line: A golden age of Chinese poetry, trade and Buddhism.
tie: Its army met the Abbasids at Talas in 751, and the first Muslim communities in China date to its age.

name: Franks and Holy Roman Empire
line: The kingdom of the Franks, which grew into Charlemagne's empire and the Holy Roman Empire.
tie: The Franks stopped the Umayyad advance at Tours (732), and Charlemagne exchanged envoys with Harun al-Rashid.

name: State of Madinah
line: The first Muslim community, led by the Prophet ﷺ after the Hijrah.
tie: Here most of the Quran's laws were revealed and the first society around a mosque was built.

name: Rashidun Caliphate
line: The rule of the four rightly guided caliphs: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali.
tie: They gathered the Quran into one book and carried Islam from Arabia to Persia, Syria and Egypt.

name: Umayyad Caliphate
line: The first dynastic caliphate, ruling from Damascus over lands from Spain to Sindh.
tie: It built the Dome of the Rock and made Arabic the language of government.

name: Abbasid Caliphate
line: The caliphate of Baghdad, home of the House of Wisdom and Islam's golden age.
tie: Under it the great hadith collections and the schools of law took shape.

name: Umayyads of Cordoba
line: Umayyad survivors who ruled al-Andalus from Cordoba, a city of libraries and lamps.
tie: Its Great Mosque and scholars made Cordoba a centre of Muslim learning in Europe.

name: Fatimid Caliphate
line: An Ismaili Shia caliphate that ruled North Africa, Egypt and Syria.
tie: It founded Cairo and al-Azhar, which later became a great centre of Sunni learning.

name: Ghaznavids
line: A Turkic dynasty of Afghanistan whose Sultan Mahmud raided deep into India.
tie: It carried Islam into the Punjab, and al-Biruni travelled with it to write his study of India.

name: Seljuk Empire
line: Turkish sultans who entered Baghdad in 1055 and revived Sunni power.
tie: Their vizier Nizam al-Mulk founded the Nizamiyya madrasas, where al-Ghazali taught.

name: Almoravids and Almohads
line: Two Berber reform movements that ruled Morocco and al-Andalus in turn.
tie: The Almoravids saved al-Andalus at Zallaqa (1086), and Ibn Rushd served the Almohad court.

name: Ayyubids
line: Salah al-Din's dynasty, ruling Egypt, Syria and Yemen.
tie: Salah al-Din retook Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187, after the Battle of Hattin.

name: Delhi Sultanate
line: Five dynasties of sultans who ruled north India from Delhi.
tie: They built the Qutb Minar and turned the Mongols back from India.

name: Mongol Empire
line: Genghis Khan's empire, the largest land empire in history.
tie: It destroyed Baghdad in 1258, yet within decades most of its western khans had become Muslim.

name: Mamluk Sultanate
line: Slave-soldier sultans of Egypt and Syria who stopped the Mongols.
tie: They won at Ain Jalut (1260), sheltered the Abbasid caliphs and guarded Makkah and Madinah.

name: Mali Empire
line: The West African empire of Mansa Musa, rich in gold and learning.
tie: Mansa Musa's hajj in 1324 made Mali famous, and Timbuktu became a city of scholars.

name: Muslim Mongol khanates
line: Mongol khanates of Iran and Central Asia whose rulers embraced Islam.
tie: Ghazan Khan became Muslim in 1295, and the heirs of Baghdad's destroyers became builders of mosques.

name: Seljuks of Rum and beyliks
line: The Seljuk sultanate of Anatolia and the Turkish beyliks that followed it.
tie: Its capital Konya was home to Rumi, and its lands became the cradle of the Ottomans.

name: Ottoman Empire
line: A Turkish dynasty that ruled across three continents for six centuries.
tie: It took Constantinople in 1453, served the Two Holy Mosques, and held the caliphate until 1924.

name: Ming and Qing China
line: China's last two imperial dynasties.
tie: The Muslim admiral Zheng He sailed for the Ming, and the Qing ruled millions of Hui and Uyghur Muslims.

name: Safavid Persia
line: A Persian dynasty that made Iran Shia and built Isfahan.
tie: It turned Iran from mostly Sunni to Twelver Shia and fought the Ottomans for two centuries.

name: Mughal Empire
line: Babur's descendants, who ruled most of the Indian subcontinent.
tie: It built the Taj Mahal and the Badshahi Mosque, and Aurangzeb sponsored the Fatawa Alamgiri.

name: European colonial empires
line: European empires that came to rule most of the Muslim world.
tie: By 1920 only a handful of Muslim lands, such as Turkey, Iran, Afghanistan and central Arabia, were free of European rule.
clio: French Mandate for Syria and Lebanon

name: Pahlavi Iran
line: Iran under the Qajar and then the Pahlavi shahs.
tie: Its shahs ruled a Shia nation squeezed between Russia and Britain, until the revolution of 1979.

name: Sokoto Caliphate
line: A West African caliphate founded by the scholar Usman dan Fodio.
tie: It grew out of a call to renew Islam and became one of Africa's largest states.

name: Saudi Arabia
line: The kingdom that unites most of Arabia, including Makkah and Madinah.
tie: It serves the Two Holy Mosques, and the King Fahd Complex in Madinah prints millions of Qurans.

name: Republic of Turkey
line: The republic that succeeded the Ottoman Empire.
tie: It abolished the caliphate in 1924, ending a line of caliphs that began with Abu Bakr.

name: Independent Muslim-majority states
line: Independent Muslim-majority countries after the end of empire.
tie: Today they meet in the OIC, and together they are home to most of the world's Muslims.

name: Cold War and after
line: The age of the American and Soviet superpowers, and the world after it.
tie: Many Muslim lands became battlefields of this rivalry, from Afghanistan to the Middle East.

name: Hittite Empire
line: A Bronze Age empire of Anatolia that rivalled Egypt.
tie: It made the oldest known peace treaty with Ramesses II, a pharaoh often proposed for the time of Musa.

name: Olmec civilisation
line: Mexico's earliest major civilisation, famous for its giant stone heads.
tie: The Quran says no nation was left without a warner (35:24), though it names none in the Americas.

name: Phoenicia
line: Seafaring cities of Lebanon, such as Tyre and Sidon, that spread the alphabet.
tie: Their alphabet is an ancestor of the Arabic script, and their god Baal is the idol Ilyas condemned (37:125).

name: Kingdom of Kush
line: A Nubian kingdom on the Nile whose kings once ruled Egypt as pharaohs.
tie: Its Nile lands became Sudan, where Islam later spread through trade, scholars and Sufi teachers.

name: Carthage
line: A Phoenician trading city in Tunisia that fought Rome for the Mediterranean.
tie: The Muslims founded Kairouan nearby in 670 and took Carthage itself in 698.

name: Minaeans, Qataban and Hadramawt
line: Incense kingdoms of ancient Yemen, neighbours and rivals of Saba.
tie: Their frankincense road ran north past Makkah, the route later travelled by Quraysh's caravans (106:2).

name: Maurya Empire
line: India's first great empire, ruled by Chandragupta and Ashoka.
tie: The Quran names no prophet in India; centuries later al-Biruni studied its faiths carefully in his book on India.

name: Nabataean Kingdom
line: Arab traders of the incense road who carved Petra and Hegra from rock.
tie: Their tombs fill al-Hijr, the old land of Thamud (15:80), and their script grew into the Arabic alphabet.

name: Parthian Empire
line: An Iranian empire that held off Rome for nearly five centuries.
tie: Its Zoroastrian faith is that of the Majus, whom the Quran names beside other religions (22:17).

name: Judea
line: The Jewish kingdom of the Hasmoneans and Herod, which became a Roman province.
tie: Zakariya, Yahya, Maryam and Isa lived in this land under Herod's family and Roman governors.

name: Maya civilisation
line: City-states of Central America with pyramids, writing and a precise calendar.
tie: Their kingdoms rose and fell long before Islam reached the Americas; the Quran says every people has a guide (13:7).

name: Gupta Empire
line: A classical Indian empire of science, art and Sanskrit literature.
tie: Indian numerals with zero, developed in this age, passed through al-Khwarizmi in Baghdad to the world as 'Arabic numerals'.

name: Lakhmid Kingdom
line: An Arab kingdom at al-Hirah in Iraq that guarded Persia's desert frontier.
tie: After Persia ended it, Arab tribes beat the Persians at Dhu Qar (c. 609), and Khalid ibn al-Walid took al-Hirah in 633.

name: Christian Nubia
line: Christian kingdoms of the middle Nile: Nobatia, Makuria and Alodia.
tie: Makuria made the Baqt treaty with the Muslims of Egypt in 652, one of the longest-lasting treaties in history.

name: Ghassanids
line: Christian Arab kings in Syria who guarded Rome's desert frontier.
tie: A Ghassanid chief killed the Prophet's ﷺ envoy, which led to the Battle of Mu'tah in 629.

name: Japan
line: The island realm of emperors and shoguns.
tie: Islam reached Japan only in the late 1800s; an Ottoman frigate's visit in 1890 was among the first contacts.

name: Christian Spain
line: The Christian kingdoms of Iberia that grew into Spain and its empire.
tie: Its Reconquista ended Muslim al-Andalus in 1492, and Spain's Muslims, the Moriscos, were expelled in 1609-1614.

name: Aghlabids
line: Emirs of Ifriqiya (Tunisia) who ruled from Kairouan for the Abbasids.
tie: They rebuilt Kairouan's Great Mosque and began the Muslim conquest of Sicily in 827.

name: Idrisids
line: The first Muslim dynasty of Morocco, founded by a descendant of the Prophet ﷺ.
tie: Idris I descended from Hasan ibn Ali, and in their city of Fez, Fatima al-Fihri founded al-Qarawiyyin in 859.

name: Khmer Empire
line: The empire of Angkor in Cambodia, builders of Angkor Wat.
tie: The Cham Muslims of Cambodia today descend largely from Champa, Angkor's old rival.

name: Samanids
line: Persian emirs of Bukhara and Samarkand who ruled Central Asia under the Abbasids.
tie: Their Bukhara was a centre of learning, where the young Ibn Sina read in the royal library.

name: Kievan Rus'
line: The first East Slavic state, ruled from Kyiv, and its principalities.
tie: The Abbasid envoy Ibn Fadlan described the Rus in 921, and a chronicle says Vladimir weighed Islam before choosing Christianity.

name: England and Britain
line: England and later the United Kingdom, centre of the largest empire in history.
tie: By 1900 it ruled more Muslims than any other state, from India to Egypt.

name: Buyids
line: Shia Daylamite emirs from Iran who controlled Baghdad and its caliphs.
tie: From 945 the Abbasid caliphs reigned under them for a century, until the Seljuks arrived in 1055.

name: Song China
line: A Chinese dynasty of printing, porcelain and great port cities.
tie: Arab and Persian Muslim merchants thrived in its port of Quanzhou, where a mosque from the Song era still stands.

name: France
line: The Kingdom of France and the republics and empires that followed it.
tie: Napoleon invaded Egypt in 1798, and France ruled Algeria from 1830 to 1962.

name: Taifa kingdoms
line: The rival kingdoms that al-Andalus broke into after the Caliphate of Cordoba fell.
tie: Their divisions let Castile take Toledo in 1085, and they called on the Almoravids for help.
clio: Taifa of Santa Maria do Algarve

name: Khwarazmian Empire
line: A Central Asian empire that briefly ruled from the Aral Sea to Iran.
tie: Its massacre of a Mongol caravan at Otrar (1218) brought Genghis Khan into the Muslim world.

name: Crusader states
line: Latin Christian states set up in Syria and Palestine by the First Crusade.
tie: They held Jerusalem from 1099 until Salah al-Din retook it in 1187; the last of them fell in 1291.

name: Great Zimbabwe
line: A southern African kingdom known for its great stone walls.
tie: Its gold reached the world through Muslim Swahili ports such as Kilwa and Sofala.

name: Zengids
line: Turkish atabegs of Mosul and Aleppo who led the fight against the Crusaders.
tie: Zengi retook Edessa in 1144, and Nur al-Din built the minbar that Salah al-Din later placed in al-Aqsa.

name: Portugal
line: An Atlantic kingdom born in the Reconquista that built a sea empire.
tie: Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498, and Portugal seized Muslim-ruled ports from Hormuz to Malacca.

name: Ghurids
line: An Afghan dynasty from the mountains of Ghor that conquered north India.
tie: Muhammad of Ghor won at Tarain in 1192, and his general Qutb al-Din Aybak founded the Delhi Sultanate.

name: Hafsids
line: Heirs of the Almohads who ruled Tunisia and eastern Algeria from Tunis.
tie: Ibn Khaldun was born in Hafsid Tunis in 1332.

name: Nasrid Granada
line: The last Muslim kingdom of al-Andalus, builders of the Alhambra.
tie: Its palace walls repeat 'There is no victor but Allah'; Granada fell in 1492.

name: Golden Horde
line: The Mongol khanate of the Russian steppe, ruled from Sarai on the Volga.
tie: Its khan Berke was among the first Mongol rulers to accept Islam, and he allied with the Mamluks against Hulagu.

name: Marinids
line: Berber sultans of Morocco who filled Fez with madrasas.
tie: Ibn Battuta set out under them in 1325 and later dictated his travels at the Marinid court.

name: Pasai and Aceh
line: Sultanates of northern Sumatra, among the first Muslim states of Southeast Asia.
tie: Ibn Battuta visited Pasai in 1345, and Aceh became known as the 'Veranda of Makkah' for its hajj pilgrims.

name: Russia
line: Muscovy, the empire of the Tsars, the Soviet Union and today's Russia.
tie: It took Kazan in 1552 and later Crimea, the Caucasus and Central Asia, ruling millions of Muslims.

name: Ifat and Adal
line: Muslim sultanates of the Horn of Africa, ruling from Zeila and later Harar.
tie: Its imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim fought Christian Ethiopia in the 1530s, in the region that had sheltered the first Muslim emigrants.

name: Deccan sultanates
line: The Bahmani sultanate of the Deccan and the five kingdoms that split from it.
tie: Its sultans built Bijapur's Gol Gumbaz and welcomed scholars from Persia and Arabia.

name: Bengal Sultanate
line: An independent sultanate of Bengal, ruling from Pandua and Gaur.
tie: Islam took deep root among Bengal's people, whose land is now one of the largest Muslim nations.

name: Timurids
line: Timur's empire and his descendants' cultured courts in Samarkand and Herat.
tie: Timur ravaged Muslim cities, yet his grandson Ulugh Beg built a great observatory and his descendant Babur founded the Mughals.

name: Malacca Sultanate
line: A Malay port sultanate on the strait between the Indian Ocean and China.
tie: Its rulers' conversion helped spread Islam across the Malay world, until Portugal took the port in 1511.

name: Aztec Empire
line: The Mexica empire of Tenochtitlan in the Valley of Mexico.
tie: It fell in 1521 to the Spain that had taken Granada from the Muslims 29 years before.

name: Inca Empire
line: The Andean empire of roads and terraces, ruled from Cusco.
tie: It fell to Spanish conquerors in 1532, a generation after the fall of Granada.

name: Songhai Empire
line: The West African empire that followed Mali along the Niger.
tie: Under Askia Muhammad, Timbuktu's scholars and the Sankore mosque flourished.

name: Kanem-Bornu
line: A Lake Chad empire ruled by one dynasty for about a thousand years.
tie: Its kings accepted Islam around 1085, making it one of Africa's oldest Muslim states.

name: Alawi Morocco
line: The dynasty that has ruled Morocco since the 1600s.
tie: Its sultans trace their line to Hasan ibn Ali, and Morocco never came under Ottoman rule.

name: Qajar Iran
line: A Turkic dynasty that ruled Iran from Tehran.
tie: Its shahs led a Shia nation that lost the Caucasus to Russia in wars between 1804 and 1828.
